pool.prompt: Under 47 CFR Part 32, where do route-survey costs (labor, drone rental, subcontract GIS firm) accumulate during the pre-construction engineering phase?
choices: Cable and Wire Facilities (account 2410) — because the survey work is for a cable project
Motor vehicle expense — because field survey requires trucks and equipment
Telecommunications Plant Under Construction (account 2003) — a temporary staging account for all in-progress project costs before the plant is placed in service
Poles (account 2411) — because the survey documents existing poles
pool.explanation: Plant Under Construction (47 CFR 32.2003) is the correct temporary account for survey and engineering costs during project development, including AFUDC (Allowance for Funds Used During Construction). Costs transfer to permanent plant accounts (2410 Cable and Wire, 2411 Poles) once the plant is placed in service.

pool.prompt: A field supervisor submits a weekly timesheet with a single line: 'Survey work, 5 days, Project XYZ.' An RUS auditor later requests source documents supporting cost allocation between Route A (aerial) and Route B (underground). What problem does this create?
choices: No problem — the summary timesheet is sufficient on its own
The accounting team cannot reconstruct the cost allocation between the two routes without original per-day, per-route source records — the lump timesheet is an audit exposure
The auditor only checks total project cost, never sub-route allocation
The problem can be corrected by submitting an amended timesheet years later
pool.explanation: An RUS plant audit traces costs back to original source documents. A lump timesheet without per-route, per-phase detail doesn't support the account allocation required by 47 CFR Part 32 — the field supervisor's timesheet should carry per-project and per-phase detail from the day of the work.

pool.prompt: What is the FCC's standardized chart of accounts that assigns a specific account number to every type of telecommunications plant and cost called?
choices: Rural Utilities Service Materials Register
Uniform System of Accounts (USOA)
Telecommunications Cost Allocation Manual
FCC Construction Standards Handbook
pool.explanation: The Uniform System of Accounts (USOA) is the core of 47 CFR Part 32. It defines every account number that RUS borrowers and FCC-regulated carriers use to classify and record plant investment and operating costs.
pool.citation: 47 CFR Part 32 — Uniform System of Accounts.

pool.prompt: You are determining how long to retain field notes and photo logs from a route survey on a RUS-funded project. What is the best approach?
choices: Keep them for 3 years, a standard contract limitation period
Keep them for 7 years, the standard IRS records retention period
Keep them for 15 years, a commonly cited FCC retention period
Confirm the applicable retention period against the current FCC records-retention schedule AND the specific RUS loan agreement, which may impose a longer period
pool.explanation: The correct retention period depends on the current FCC retention schedule and the specific RUS loan agreement, which can extend the required period beyond any FCC minimum. Hardcoding a specific number of years without verifying current regulation and loan agreement terms is risky.
pool.citation: 47 CFR 32.27 (records retention); 7 CFR Part 1755 (RUS loan requirements) — for the exact FCC Part 42 retention schedule figure, confirm with regulatory counsel or the RUS district office.

pool.prompt: Once a project's plant is placed in service, what happens to the costs that had accumulated in the Plant Under Construction account (47 CFR 32.2003)?
choices: They are written off entirely and never appear in any permanent account

They are transferred from the temporary Plant Under Construction account into the appropriate permanent plant accounts (e.g., Cable and Wire Facilities, Poles) that reflect the actual type of installed infrastructure
They remain permanently in account 2003 regardless of project completion
They are automatically converted into a separate depreciation reserve account with no further tracking
pool.explanation: Account 2003 is explicitly a temporary staging account for costs before the plant is placed in service. Once construction completes and the plant enters service, the accumulated costs move to the permanent plant accounts matching the actual installed infrastructure type.

pool.prompt: Why does the Uniform System of Accounts (USOA) matter to a field survey crew, who might assume accounting is purely an office-side concern?
choices: It doesn't matter at all — field crews have no role in accurate cost accounting

How a field crew documents and timesheets their work (project, phase, route segment) directly determines whether the accounting team can correctly allocate costs to the right USOA accounts — sloppy field documentation creates downstream audit exposure regardless of good field survey work quality
USOA account numbers are automatically assigned by GPS coordinates with no human input
USOA only applies to construction costs, never to survey/engineering costs
pool.explanation: Field-level documentation (which project, which route, which phase) is the raw source data the accounting team relies on to correctly allocate costs into USOA accounts — a disconnect between field documentation practice and USOA requirements creates real audit exposure even when the underlying survey work itself was done well.

pool.prompt: An RUS auditor challenges a project's cost allocation because timesheets lack per-route detail. What single change to field documentation practice would have prevented this audit finding?
choices: Nothing could have prevented it; RUS audits always find some issue
Recording per-day, per-route (or per-phase) detail on timesheets from the start, rather than a single lump-sum daily entry covering the whole project
Switching from paper timesheets to digital timesheets, regardless of the level of detail recorded
Having the project manager sign off on timesheets weekly instead of daily
pool.explanation: The core issue is granularity, not format or approval workflow — a timesheet needs per-route/per-phase detail captured at the time of the work for the accounting team to defensibly allocate costs to the correct accounts and routes.

pool.prompt: Why should a field supervisor never assume the '15 years' or '7 years' retention figures sometimes cited informally are correct for a specific RUS project's field notes?
choices: Because retention periods are always exactly 3 years with no exceptions

Because the actual applicable period depends on the CURRENT FCC retention schedule (which can change) AND the specific RUS loan agreement's terms (which can impose a longer period than any general FCC minimum) — an informally-remembered number can be outdated or simply wrong for that specific project
Because retention periods only apply to accounting records, never to field survey notes
Because RUS project records never require any retention period at all
pool.explanation: Retention requirements are a moving target across two independent sources (the current regulatory schedule and the specific loan agreement's terms) — treating a remembered figure as authoritative risks being wrong in either direction, which is why verifying against current sources for the specific project is the correct practice.
